title: AI at work: jobs that change
essentialQuestion: How might AI change people's jobs, and who gains or loses?
learningGoal: Use examples from history to explain how new machines change work, and describe who might gain or lose as AI changes jobs.

warmUp.question: A new machine can do part of a worker's job. What do you think happens to the worker?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: For each worker, which tasks changed? Who gained, and who lost?

cards.title: Three workers in the town of Millbrook

cases.name: Clerks at the water office
cases.body: Ines and two other clerks typed up customer forms. Now an AI tool reads most forms and fills in the details. The office needs fewer clerks. After some training, Ines and one other clerk moved to the help desk, where they help people with hard problems. The third clerk lost her work.

cases.name: Teacher at the learning centre
cases.body: Ms Rana uses an AI tool to make practice questions. She checks every question, because the tool sometimes makes mistakes. She now has more time to help learners one by one.

cases.name: Tailor at the market
cases.body: Sami makes and mends clothes. A translation tool helps him talk with customers who speak other languages, so he has more customers. The tool can't sew, and it can't measure a person.

activity.title: AI or a person?
activity.instructions: Put each task into a group. There is no score. After you place one, you can see one possible answer and the reason.

items.feedback: It is the same simple step again and again, which machines do well.

items.text: Comforting a child who is upset
items.feedback: Care and kindness come from people. A child needs someone who knows them and can stay with them.

items.text: Fixing a broken water pipe in a house
items.feedback: Every house is different, and the work needs skilled hands.

items.text: Translating a shop sign into another language
items.feedback: A tool can translate fast, but a speaker should check it. Tools make more mistakes in some languages.

items.text: Finding the photos that show a tree among 5,000 photos
items.feedback: Tools that find patterns in photos can do this quickly. A person might still check the ones the tool was not sure about.

items.text: Choosing which new player joins the football team
items.feedback: Choices about people should be made by people who can explain them. AI can be unfair, as Lesson 8 showed. You could say both, if a tool only helps to collect facts.

items.text: Making practice questions for a class
items.feedback: A tool can make questions fast. The teacher checks them, like Ms Rana in Millbrook.

items.text: Writing the first draft of a letter
items.feedback: Any group can be right here. A tool can write a first draft. A person decides what the letter should say, and checks it.

activity.saves: The group the learner chose for each task, with the lesson's other answers.
activity.offline: Everything is in the lesson file. Nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.heading: New machines have changed work before
sections.text: AI is not the first technology to change people's work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in factories began to do work that skilled cloth workers had done by hand. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, called Luddites, broke machines in protest. The machines were taking their work. Much later, from the 1970s, cash machines slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, who handle money at the counter, to disappear. But a study from 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed about the same and even grew a little. Banks opened more branches, and tellers spent more time helping customers. That was one machine, long ago, so it can't tell us what AI will do.
sections.simpler: AI is not the first technology to change work. In the 1800s, new machines in England did the work of skilled cloth workers. Workers called Luddites broke some machines. From the 1970s, banks in the United States got cash machines. Many thought bank workers at the counter would disappear. A 2015 study found there were still about as many. Banks opened more branches, and workers helped customers more. That was long ago. It can't tell us what AI will do.

sections.heading: AI changes tasks inside jobs
sections.text: Most jobs are made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets came to office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work. Yet the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for work, found that about one in four jobs in the world has some exposure to AI tools that write and make things. This means these tools could do some of the tasks in those jobs. It is not a count of jobs lost. Office jobs, such as clerks, have the most exposure. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear.
sections.simpler: A job is made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, not the whole job. Spreadsheets did sums for office workers. Some people who added up numbers lost their work. But there were more accountants. In 2025, a United Nations group studied AI that writes and makes things. About one in four jobs has some exposure to it. It could do some of their tasks. This is not a count of lost jobs. Office jobs have the most exposure. Most will likely change, not disappear.

sections.heading: Some people gain, and some people lose
sections.text: Change at work is often uneven. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund warned that AI could help some workers do more, and take important tasks from others. It also said AI will probably make inequality worse unless governments act. In Millbrook, the water office works faster. Two clerks moved to the help desk after training, but one lost her work. Training and fair rules can help. Workers, employers and governments can decide together how new tools are used.
sections.simpler: In 2024, money experts said AI may help some workers. It may take big tasks from others. It may make inequality worse, unless leaders act. After training, two Millbrook clerks moved to the help desk. One lost her work. Training and fair rules can help. Workers and leaders can decide together how to use AI.

glossary.definition: Tools and machines that people make to solve problems.

glossary.example: The water office used AI to automate reading forms.

glossary.definition: One piece of work that is part of a job.

glossary.example: Office jobs have the most exposure to AI tools that write.

checks.question: What happened to bank tellers in the United States as cash machines spread?

options.text: Their work changed to helping customers
options.feedback: Yes. A 2015 study found about as many tellers, and they spent more time helping customers.

options.text: All of the tellers lost their work
options.feedback: Not quite. Many people expected this, but it didn't happen. Read the end of the first section.

options.text: Tellers began to build cash machines
options.feedback: Not quite. Tellers still worked in banks. Read what they spent more time doing.

checks.question: The ILO says most jobs with some exposure to these tools are more likely to ...

options.text: disappear in a year or two
options.feedback: Not quite. The study says something else. Read the end of the second section.

options.text: change, because people are still needed
options.feedback: Yes. The tools could do some tasks, but people are still needed for many others.

options.text: stay exactly the same as before
options.feedback: Not quite. Many of these jobs will change. Read what the study says in the second section.

write.prompt: Choose one Millbrook worker. Explain how AI changed their work, who gained or lost, and one thing that would make the change fairer.
sentenceStarters: One thing that would make it fairer is ...
selfCheck: I named one worker and how AI changed their work.
I said who gained or who lost.
I gave one way to make the change fairer.
write.example: I chose the clerks at the Millbrook water office. AI changed their work because a new tool now reads most forms. The office gained, because the work is faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost out, because she has no work there now. This is like the cloth workers in the 1800s. One thing that would make it fairer is training for every clerk, so nobody is left without work.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner names a task from the activity. You say if AI could help, a person is still needed, or both, and why. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud what happened to bank tellers when cash machines came. Then say why that old example can't tell us for sure what AI will do.

watch.title: The big debate about the future of work, explained
watch.why: It looks back at a hundred years of worry about machines taking jobs, and asks who gains from new technology.
watch.beforeQuestion: Do you think new machines make more jobs or fewer jobs? Why?
watch.afterQuestion: Why does the video say that who gains from technology depends on people's choices?
watch.summary: This video asks if machines and AI will take away people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. It happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology makes some new jobs, such as building and fixing machines. It also makes things cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because it can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.
keyPoints: People have worried about machines taking jobs many times before.
New technology removes some jobs but also helps create new ones.
Who gains from technology depends on the rules and choices people make.
watch.contentNote: Vox, 2017: made before today's AI chat tools, and about the United States. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed (October 2026); the length, about 9 minutes, comes from Rosetta's transcript archive and is not confirmed on YouTube. It mentions IBM's Watson, a 2013 Oxford study and US income figures. The summary was written from that archive's transcript summary, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it before use; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Many learners may not be allowed to work where they live, and work and money can be painful topics for families. Never ask learners about their own or their family's jobs, income or plans for work. The lesson uses made-up Millbrook workers, and the think question lets learners pick a machine from the lesson.
Britannica notes that the government punished the Luddites harshly, including hangings. The lesson leaves this out; if learners ask, keep it short and factual.
educatorNotes: One exposure figure in learner text, on purpose. The ILO's (May 2025, with Poland's NASK) is potential exposure to generative AI: 25% of the world's jobs are in occupations where these tools could do some tasks. It is not a count of jobs lost, and the ILO expects most to be transformed rather than replaced; clerical jobs are the most exposed, and in rich countries the jobs most at risk of automation are 9.6% of women's jobs against 3.5% of men's. The IMF's figure (January 2024) has a wider scope: almost 40% of the world's jobs, and about 60% in advanced economies, are exposed to AI in general, with roughly half of those likely to gain and half to see lower demand. Learner text keeps only the IMF's warning about inequality, without its numbers, so the two estimates aren't mixed up. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015); it shows one past case, not a forecast for AI. The spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015).

Paper version of the activity: write the eight tasks on cards and sort them under the three headings. There is no score; reward reasons. A teacher could add a local example of a tool that changed work, without asking about anyone's own job.
changes: New lesson (Digital World, October 2026, social studies rebuild). There is no Base44 original, so oldId is null. Lesson 9 in “AI in daily life” (ai-in-daily-life).

Social studies angle with history: cloth machines and the Luddites (1811–1816), cash machines and bank tellers, spreadsheets and bookkeepers, then the ILO's 2025 and the IMF's 2024 findings on AI and jobs, and who gains or loses.
Adds a sort activity: tasks into “AI could help with this”, “A person is still needed” and “Both”. All workers and tasks learners work with are made up (Millbrook).
